Cloud economics is becoming compute economics
Cloud economics draaide jarenlang om geb: Cloud economics used to be about usage: consume more, pay more. AI workloads depend on expensive GPUs, reserved capacity and long-term infrastructure commitments. Companies are therefore no longer only paying for what they use, but also committing to compute capacity in advance. The FinOps question shifts from “what are we spending?” to “what compute are we committing to, and are we using it efficiently?”
Wat verandert er door AI aan cloudkosten: What does AI change about cloud costs?
Jarenlang ging cloud economics vooral ov: For years, cloud economics was mainly about usage. Consume more, pay more. AI changes that. AI workloads increasingly depend on expensive GPUs, reserved capacity and long-term infrastructure commitments.
Waarom worden commitments belangrijker?: Why do commitments become more important?
Bedrijven betalen niet langer alleen voo: Companies are no longer only paying for what they use. They also commit to compute up front. That means unused capacity costs as much as used capacity, and the risk of waste moves from individual resources to the size and duration of the commitment. For how commitment discounts work, read {1}Reserved Instances vs. Savings Plans{/1}.
Reuters meldde op 29 september 2026 dat: Reuters reported on 29 September 2026 that Anthropic has committed at least $518B to AI infrastructure over the next decade. That is an extreme example, but it shows the direction: capacity is committed in advance rather than only paid for afterwards.

{1}{2}Aan welke compute-capaciteit zijn: {1}{2}What compute capacity are we committed to, and for how long?{/2}

Bij AI hangen kosten vaker samen met dur: With AI, costs are more often tied to expensive GPUs and long-term capacity commitments. You therefore also pay for capacity you are not yet, or not fully, using.
